pinterest.title: Wedding Centrepieces: How to Choose for Your Table Shape and Room
pinterest.description: Choose wedding centrepieces for the tables you actually have. A round table asks for one focal point that reads well from every seat. A long banquet table asks for a continuous run: a garland, repeating low vessels or clusters with candles between. Keep arrangements low enough to talk over, or lift them well above seated eye level on a slim stand, never in between. Wedding centrepiece ideas grouped by style, from low florals to candlelit and non floral.

pinterest.title: Candlelit Wedding Centrepieces for Long Tables: Tapers, Hurricanes and Garlands
pinterest.description: Candles change a wedding table more than any flower once the sun goes down. Thread a foliage garland with taper candles, set pillar candles inside hurricane glass on terraces, or mass votives around a modest arrangement. Keep dried grasses, paper menus and trailing greenery well clear of the flame, use sturdy holders that will not tip over, and ask your venue about open flame first. Where flame is restricted, battery-operated candles keep the glow.

pinterest.title: Non Floral Wedding Centrepieces: Olive Branches, Lemons, Ceramics and Local Vessels
pinterest.description: Non floral wedding centrepieces that tie the table to its place. Lay loose olive branches down a terrace table with lemons and low candles, group sculptural ceramics in tonal glazes, or build each piece around vessels chosen at your destination, such as painted ceramics, copper or woven baskets. For an Australian wedding, the sculptural red waratah makes a bold native centrepiece with banksia and gum leaves, and its flowering is concentrated in spring.

slides: Your saved centrepiece photos were styled for someone else's table. Here is how to choose for yours.
Start with table shape. A round table asks for one focal piece that reads well from every seat. A long table asks for a continuous run.
Mind the sightlines. Keep it low enough to talk over, or lift it well above seated eye level on a slim stand. Never the wall of flowers at face level.
Scale it to the room. A low garden bowl that feels generous in a courtyard can disappear in a ballroom with a soaring ceiling.
Use stems well. Let foliage do more of the work, fill length with candles and greenery, and move ceremony arrangements to the reception.
Look beyond flowers. Olive branches and lemons, sculptural ceramics, lanterns, mirrored plinths, or small cakes as each table's focal point.
Ask your venue first: open flame, set-up and pack-down, and which vessels, stands and candle holders they hold.
Planning your tables from afar? Talk it through with a Wedded Advisor. Link in bio.
instagram_carousel.caption:
The centrepiece that stops you scrolling was styled for one room, one table shape and one light. Yours may need something different.

Start with the table. A round table asks for a single focal point with no back side. A long banquet table asks for a continuous line: a foliage garland, a rhythm of repeating low vessels, or clusters with candles between.

Then the rule that matters most: guests need to see and speak to the person opposite. Keep arrangements low enough to talk over, or lift them well above seated eye level on a slim stand.

Stems are the expensive part of most arrangements, so use fewer of them well. Let foliage do more of the work, fill long tables with candles and greenery, and move ceremony arrangements to the reception rather than buying twice.

And before you fall for a design, ask your venue about open flame, set-up and pack-down.

Our new guide has wedding centrepiece ideas grouped by style, from low and lush florals and candlelit runs to olive branches, lemons and sculptural ceramics, plus the questions to ask your venue and a local florist.

Read it via the link in bio, or tell us about your tables below. A Wedded Advisor is happy to talk it through.
